clinicalPearls: Progressive impairment of impulse conduction through the His-Purkinje system, causing widening QRS and heart block
It presents with syncope, bradycardia or sudden death, and may be familial or degenerative
The inherited form is associated with SCN5A and other conduction-gene mutations and can present at a younger age
SCN5A mutations link it to an overlap spectrum with Brugada syndrome and other sodium-channel disorders
It differs from age-related conduction fibrosis chiefly by earlier onset and family history
A permanent pacemaker is the mainstay of treatment for symptomatic or high-grade conduction block
reference.pathophysiology: Progressive cardiac conduction disease results from progressive fibrosis and functional impairment of the specialised conduction tissue. In inherited forms, mutations in genes encoding the cardiac sodium channel (SCN5A) and other conduction-related proteins reduce conduction reserve, so conduction slows and blocks over time, producing bundle branch block, then higher-grade atrioventricular block. Age-related degeneration (Lenegre-Lev disease) causes a similar picture through sclerosis of the conduction system. The shared SCN5A basis explains overlap with Brugada syndrome in some families.
additionalDifferentials: Cardiomyopathy with conduction disease (for example laminopathy)
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography and, where indicated, cardiac MRI to exclude structural or infiltrative disease
Genetic testing (for example SCN5A) in early-onset or familial cases
redFlags: Family history of sudden death or pacemakers at a young age
Associated structural or infiltrative cardiac disease
reference.prognosis: With timely pacing, symptomatic conduction disease is well managed; prognosis otherwise depends on associated arrhythmic risk and any underlying cardiomyopathy or channelopathy.
pitfalls: Attributing early-onset conduction disease to ageing and missing a genetic cause
Overlooking an infiltrative cardiomyopathy such as sarcoidosis
Missing associated Brugada-type risk in SCN5A families
management: Permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment for symptomatic bradycardia or high-grade conduction block

No pharmacological therapy corrects the underlying conduction failure; avoid drugs that slow conduction such as class I antiarrhythmics and atrioventricular-nodal blocking agents unless clearly indicated
Consider defibrillator therapy where an overlapping Brugada phenotype or an underlying cardiomyopathy adds arrhythmic risk
Serial ECGs and ambulatory monitoring to document progression and detect intermittent block
Echocardiography and, where indicated, cardiac MRI to exclude structural or infiltrative disease
Genetic testing such as SCN5A in early-onset or familial cases, with cascade family screening and counselling
Educate on syncope and escalate urgently for pacing when complete heart block develops
